quote: 96% of jewel beetles were attracted by light at 590 nm and ca. 87% of them still responded to light at 645 nm (C. dimidiata: 100% and 96%; C. favopicta, 93% and 78%; … ) (Fig. S1).
value: positive phototaxis to narrow-band LED light: 100% of beetles attracted at 590 nm and 96% at 645 nm
conditions: 16 C. dimidiata of 28 beetles from 2 species completed the 6-wavelength series (590 to 735 nm); wild-collected at Wombargo; tested range 590 to 735 nm, so 590 nm is the short end of the stimulus set and the paper states no shorter-wavelength response; beetle responses were attracted or not attracted, with a logistic response curve fitted per species; light intensity of the bi-choice test not stated in the page text; pooled figure in the same sentence (96% and ca. 87% of all beetles) is not used here. Contrary or limiting results in the same paper: only one C. dimidiata individual responded at 735 nm, which the authors say might be random movement; compared with the dark arm, C. dimidiata reached the lit-arm choice zone 19 times more often (C. flavopicta 5 times).
note: Accepted name Castiarina dimidiata (Carter, 1908) per Australian Faunal Directory (biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Castiarina_dimidiata, opened). Sentence seen whole on two fetches of the repository PDF text. Other sentences of the paper (50% response rate near 704 nm for C. dimidiata; 735 nm response) carry PDF ligature losses in this copy ('Te', 'Tere'), so they are not quoted. Records only the 590 and 645 nm responses, not the 704 nm figure.

source.title: Conserved visual capacity of rats under red light

where: Results, first paragraph on performance across wavelengths, eLife 10: e66429 PDF; the PDF prints 'distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License'; Crossref lists CC BY 4.0, volume 10, article e66429, issued 2021-07-20 (no issue)
value: orientation discrimination accuracy 84 ± 3% under 626 nm, 72 ± 3% under 729 nm and 50 ± 1% (chance) under 930 nm LED light
method: behavioural: rats judged whether a physical black and white square-wave grating (9.8 cm diameter circle, 3D-printed, on a stepper motor) was horizontal or vertical (0 to 45 deg rewarded as horizontal, 45 to 90 deg as vertical), choosing a left or right spout by head turn and licking; illumination by monochrome LED arrays, peak 626, 652, 729, 854 and 930 nm, against a white LED array
conditions: four male Long-Evans rats (Charles River, Calco, Italy), illumination arrays not matched for power: integrated irradiance 0.12 (626 nm), 0.28 (652 nm), 0.04 (729 nm), 1.95 (854 nm) and 0.48 mW/cm2 (930 nm) (Figure 1 caption), so the 729 nm array, where accuracy first fell, was the dimmest and wavelength and irradiance change together across the red series; the paper does not address the lower 729 nm power; dark-adapted in a light-free room for 20 to 30 min before each session, 4 to 6 weeks of training with one session a day; mean accuracy of 87 ± 2% (SEM across rats) under white light; values are group means, p against white light 0.158 (626 nm), 0.419 (652 nm), 0.00 (729 nm); 854 nm and 930 nm did not differ from chance (p=0.257, 0.316); the 854 and 930 nm LEDs emitted about 2 to 50 times more light at shorter wavelengths than the red LEDs, yet performance at those two was at chance, which the authors use to argue the red result is not leakage. Tested range 626 to 930 nm only; the study does not include direct measures of photoreceptor sensitivity.
quote: Average performance was 84 ± 3% under 626 nm illumination … 72 ± 3% under 729 nm … and 50 ± 1% under 930 nm average performance (p=0.316 compared to chance).
note: Printed 'Long-Evans rats'; Rattus norvegicus is the species (laboratory strain). Behavioural performance under narrow-band light is a task result, not a measured receptor peak, so no lambda max is claimed. Sentence reassembled from consecutive segments on two fetches; omissions marked. Trial counts per rat are not reported in the text. The same sentence also gives 86 ± 2% at 652 nm and 53 ± 2% at 854 nm (p=0.257 against chance); those parts are omitted from the quote and not claimed in the value.

method: histology: 12 micrometre dorsoventral retinal cryosections, cone density and outer segment length measured on at least four sections per animal; the visual streak is compared with dorsal and ventral peripheral retina taken about 300 micrometres from the streak centre
value: visual streak (dorsally located horizontal band); cone density (cones per 100 µm of section) 27.29% ± 9.99% higher than in adjacent peripheral retina
conditions: Figure 7D: visual streak n = 3 against adjacent peripheral retina n = 3 (animals per the legend); the paper used 9 adult gerbils aged 2 to 3 months in all and does not say which were sectioned; one-tailed paired t-test, streak normalized to periphery, error bars SD. Limiting results in the same paper: rod density was not increased in the streak despite longer rod outer segments, and the number of outer nuclear layer rows did not differ between streak and periphery. Peak cone density in absolute terms is not given in the sentence and no acuity is measured.
quote: In accordance with this view, we also found that the density of cones in the visual streak of the MG retina was increased by 27.29% ± 9.99% in comparison to the adjacent peripheral retina (Figure 7D).
note: The paper abbreviates the Mongolian gerbil as MG. The visual streak is located dorsally as a horizontal band (Section 3.6, Figure 6A). Sentence seen whole on two fetches of the PDF.
